video_title: US Home Prices Set To Fall Faster Than Even The Bears Expected | Melody Wright
gist: Housing analyst Melody Wright says US home prices just turned negative year-over-year nationally (Redfin October data) for the first time in three years and could fall faster than expected into Q1 2027 as FHA-led foreclosures accelerate, upper-K buyers retreat, and permit/financing problems at Texas data center projects threaten boom-town markets like Abilene; she calls 2027 the start of the distressed seller. The New Harbor segment covers de-risking equities, a brutal precious-metals shakeout, and 5%+ Treasury yields.

themes.theme: National home prices turn negative; foreclosures drive acceleration

insights.claim: Redfin's October sales data showed year-over-year national home prices turning negative for the first time in three years, which Melody Wright calls a very significant corner.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Signals the national housing correction has moved from forecast to measured reality.
insights.quote: for the first time in three years we have year-over-year national negative home prices

insights.claim: Melody Wright now expects US home price declines to accelerate faster than she had anticipated, potentially as soon as Q1 2027, if a stock market correction and a data center pullback compound rising foreclosures.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Shortens the timeline for her previously 'slow grind' bearish housing call.
insights.quote: we could re really be looking at acceleration in Q1 faster than I would have anticipated

insights.claim: Wright contrasts today with 2023: then, year-over-year negative prices were halted by SVB, the BTFP and Nvidia mania, and medians floated up because mostly higher-priced homes transacted; now insurance, property taxes and electricity costs are much higher and foreclosure sales are large enough to drag medians down.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: The forces that stopped the 2023 decline are absent and new cost/forced-sale pressures are present.

insights.claim: Foreclosure sales are now making a dent in median prices because regular sales are pulling back more significantly than in 2023 as rates rise, while forced sales increase, reversing the mix effect that held medians up for years.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Composition of sales is flipping from high-end-supported to distress-weighted, pushing reported medians lower.
insights.quote: It's making a dent. It's and it's making a dent because here's what's happening. Rates are going up.

insights.claim: The FHA cohort is a key source of accelerating foreclosures; restrictions imposed on FHA loss mitigation in October 2025 take this long to bite, and borrowers will exhaust their options by end of Q4 2026/Q1 2027.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: FHA-heavy markets and lenders face rising forced sales into early 2027.
insights.quote: those restrictions that went on the FHA last year in October 2025, it takes this long for that to make a difference

insights.claim: Wright frames 2026 as the year of the motivated seller and 2027 as the beginning of the distressed seller.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Expect more forced listings and price cuts through 2027.
insights.quote: 27 is going to be the beginning of the distress seller

insights.claim: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac prime portfolios started showing early delinquency in the summer; Wright expects it to show up clearly in the numbers in about 12 to 18 months despite remaining loss mitigation options.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Distress is spreading from FHA/non-QM into prime agency credit.

insights.claim: Wright expects foreclosure sales to reach 2007 levels by around Q2 2027, at which point the national downturn will be undeniable.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: A visible inflection that could shift mainstream narrative and policy response by mid-2027.
insights.quote: when we get to 2007 level of actual foreclosure sales, which I think we'll probably get there by Q2 of next year

insights.claim: The Black Knight/ICE delinquency report for last month acknowledged delinquencies are back at 2019 levels, which commentators wrongly dismiss as a return to norms.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: The 'normalization' narrative masks an ongoing upward trend in delinquency.
insights.quote: we are now back at 2019 levels

insights.claim: Any foreclosure moratorium (the 2011-style 'regulatory playbook') would come too late to stop the decline, because many investors are already walking away and handing back keys to dozens of single-family homes regardless.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Don't count on policy to put a floor under prices.
insights.quote: the horse has already left the barn

insights.claim: Wright says the only thing that could arrest the national housing downturn would be large pay raises plus bringing missing workers back into the labor force.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Watch wage growth and labor participation as the key reversal signals.
insights.quote: Unless we all get huge payraises and we bring those missing people from the workforce back in

themes.theme: Data center boom towns: Texas permits, financing stress and fragile local markets

insights.claim: New officials elected in the recent blue wave with anti-data-center or pro-regulation agendas pose a significant threat to data center construction jobs and, by extension, boom-town housing markets that have offset national weakness.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Data-center-driven local housing markets are a key weak link in the bull case.

insights.claim: Wright cites a Goldman Sachs study estimating 45% of data center projects could be impacted, with about 25% of that in Texas.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Texas is the epicenter of regulatory risk to the AI buildout.
insights.quote: Goldman Sachs did a study and said 45% of projects could be impacted

insights.claim: Most Texas data center projects are 'behind the meter', building their own gas power plants, but many got started on minor air permits (the kind used for a dry cleaner) when they actually need major air permits, so permits are now in question and could be denied or delayed.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Permitting is an under-appreciated Achilles heel for the AI capex cycle; even delays hurt.
insights.quote: they kind of cheated and got what's called a minor air permit to get started

insights.claim: At Stargate Abilene the construction workforce peaked around 9,000 and is already rolling over, partly because Microsoft's planned expansion lacks a permit.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Early sign that data center construction employment has peaked locally.

insights.claim: Abilene, Texas (population ~130,000) has home prices up 26% year over year and median rent of $2,600 versus a US median of $1,400, showing how data center booms distort local housing.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Boom-town housing is highly exposed if construction crews leave.
insights.quote: home prices are up 26% year-over-year in a town of 130,000 people

insights.claim: On her 2,000-mile Texas data center road trip, Wright found boom-town excess (a $447 Courtyard Marriott night in Abilene, $13 food-truck lemonade at the Shackelford site) while hotels and restaurants elsewhere were empty, explaining how data center spending is propping up the economy.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Economic resilience is concentrated in data center towns and is fragile.

insights.claim: Data center developers are running out of money: mechanics liens are being filed against Vantage projects because contractors aren't paid fast enough, and Vantage faces a federal lawsuit in San Antonio over permitting.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Liquidity stress, not politics, is the bigger near-term threat to the buildout.
insights.quote: all these people are running out of money

insights.claim: Neocloud projects relying on private financing are stalling; Wright visited a Cloudburst site where construction had barely begun as private financing dries up.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Smaller AI infrastructure players are the most vulnerable to a credit pullback.

insights.claim: A short-term rental operator in Abilene saw occupancy fall about 20% from roughly 83% over several months, after Abilene had been the top small Airbnb market last year.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Boom-town demand is already fading quickly.
insights.quote: They've seen over the last several months about a 20% drop in that occupancy

insights.claim: Wright argues the debt markets, not politicians, will decide the data center buildout's fate, and that Oracle credit default swaps are not yet wide enough given how exposed Oracle is.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Oracle credit looks mispriced relative to its data center exposure.
insights.quote: those credit default swaps are not wide enough on Oracle yet cuz they are so exposed here

insights.claim: Project Jupiter, the Oracle/OpenAI site on the Texas-New Mexico border, was denied a local pipeline, obtained expedited federal approval, and is now being challenged by the New Mexico attorney general, illustrating that even federal rescue still means delay.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Federal intervention can't fully prevent delays.

insights.claim: Wright expects the federal government may step in to buy land or save some data center projects, but sees significant delays regardless because many operators 'want out' as their balance sheets bleed and diesel costs rise.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Headwinds are more likely than a rescue-driven acceleration.
insights.quote: I think there are people that want out, Adam. They want out because they are drowning.

themes.theme: Credit stress seen from the mortgage servicing back end

insights.claim: At a Dallas mortgage servicing conference, servicers broadly confirmed Wright's bearish outlook and said loans the agencies sold to hedge funds are not reporting to credit, hiding true delinquency.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Official delinquency data likely understates actual distress.
insights.quote: all of those sales out into that the agencies did off to the hedge funds are not reporting to credit

insights.claim: Wright notes non-qualified (non-QM) private mortgages were about 12% delinquent last year, and servicer reactions suggested current conditions are worse than she thought.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Non-QM credit is a hot spot for losses.

insights.claim: REO vendors told Wright they processed as many real-estate-owned properties in the last two months as in the prior two years, alongside exponential increases in bankruptcies and skyrocketing short sales.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Rate of change in bank-owned inventory is spiking—a leading indicator of price pressure.
insights.quote: we did in the last two months, we did as many AROs as we've done in the last two years

insights.claim: Wright, echoing Steve Eisman, argues the REIT, multifamily and Airbnb operators who came from Wall Street around 2016 don't understand credit, while seasoned back-end servicing staff do and are preparing for trouble.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Look to downstream credit people, not originators/sell side, for early warning.

insights.claim: Wright expects the mortgage credit/delinquency story to enter public view by year-end 2026 or Q1 2027.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Media narrative shift could hit housing sentiment and related equities.

insights.claim: Mainstream outlets (Wall Street Journal and Realtor.com, which share a parent) have started telling boomers to consider selling and saying second-home ownership no longer makes sense, which Wright sees as a notable shift.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Sell-side housing media turning cautious is a sentiment tell.

insights.claim: Existing home sales show massive year-over-year declines in the $500,000 to $1 million segment ('middle of the upper K'), which had been propping up the median sales price.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Loss of upper-middle buyers removes a key support for national medians.

insights.claim: Multifamily syndications where LPs (often doctors and dentists) aren't being paid are now pervasive as 2021-vintage borrowers hit a debt maturity wall without the refinancing they counted on; the same applies to commercial real estate and vehicles like Blue Owl.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: High-net-worth wealth losses feed into reduced housing demand and forced sales.
insights.quote: you're hitting that hard debt maturity wall

insights.claim: Consumer spending is rising only because staples and gas cost more, with credit card balances growing because people can't afford everyday life; Home Depot and consumer staples companies are flashing warnings.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Nominal spending strength masks consumer stress.

insights.claim: Citing Parcl, Wright says for every two vacation homes sold only one is bought, as boomers offload non-essential properties in a risk-off move; luxury markets and spec homes (e.g. an unsold $25M+ spec flip) are struggling.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Second-home and luxury markets face supply overhang.
insights.quote: for every two vacation homes that are sold, one is bought

insights.claim: Private credit is still lending on short-term rental investment properties, which is why more STR owners haven't sold yet; when that stops, selling will intensify.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: A private-credit pullback is a trigger for STR liquidations.
insights.quote: because private credit is still flowing

insights.claim: Wright expects a stock market correction based on what she saw on the road, which would push high-net-worth owners to list vacation homes immediately and worsen the housing story.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Equity and housing downside are linked through wealth effects.

themes.theme: Practical housing playbook by life stage

insights.claim: For older owners with a 1-2 year horizon to downsize, Wright advises list, sell and rent rather than wait, asking 'who could buy my home?' rather than trusting automated estimates.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Sellers with time pressure should get ahead of the decline.
insights.quote: So list, sell, and rent would be the answer for most people.

insights.claim: Rents are firming somewhat because people 65+ are the biggest cohort adding to rentals as they exit ownership, though concessions like three months free are still common.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Rental market is not collapsing; downsizers support rent demand.

insights.claim: For first-time buyers, Wright says now is not the time to buy; use this as a planning period to pick location and home type and be ready when conditions turn.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Patience favors buyers.
insights.quote: No, this is not the time to jump in.

insights.claim: For owners without plans to sell, Wright's priority is paying down debt as fast as possible, starting with high-interest credit cards, while keeping low-rate mortgages and watching for refinancing opportunities.
insights.speaker: Melody Wright
insights.so_what: Those with debt will suffer most in the coming downturn.
insights.quote: those with debt I think are going to suffer the most

insights.claim: Adam Taggart suggests young buyers use tools like Foreclosure.com and PropertyRadar to find distressed owners (liens, pre-foreclosure) and make below-market offers backed by Reventure data.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Distress creates off-market buying opportunities for prepared buyers.

insights.claim: New Harbor's John Lod says housing is in the early throes of a broad-based selloff after years of distorting monetary policy, noting Massachusetts, considered resilient, now has more inventory, longer days on market and price cuts.
insights.speaker: John Lod (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Even 'resilient' markets are weakening.

insights.claim: Mike Preston expects home prices perhaps 20-30% lower and stocks potentially down 60% in the next big downturn to return to normal valuations, noting Austin is likely closer to its bottom than most since it already got crushed.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Large downside remains in both housing and equities; local timing varies.
insights.quote: prices should be lower, maybe 30 20 to 30% lower in the next big downturn

themes.theme: Markets, precious metals and bonds (New Harbor segment)

insights.claim: Mike Preston says the S&P 500 has chopped between about 7,300 and 7,700 for six months with a textbook rally to the 50-day moving average and rollover, and the market is roughly three times normal valuations.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Range-bound, overvalued market with failing momentum breakouts.
insights.quote: we've been going between about 7,300 and 7,700 for 6 months

insights.claim: New Harbor's system flipped back to full defense, cutting equity exposure from 50% to 42.5% to 38.5% and now 34.5%, adding call options and collars as hedges; healthcare and software were recent additions as relatively strong sectors.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Systematic managers are de-risking despite blowoff-top possibility.

insights.claim: Preston still leans toward a possible blowoff top (citing Felix Zulauf's S&P ~8,000 call) and sees up to ~9,000 possible, noting the unusually rapid surge of fear on a 6-8% pullback may be 'loading the chamber' for a rally.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Fear spikes can fuel rallies, but positioning should stay measured.

insights.claim: Silver (SLV) is down about 60-65% from its high and gold about 30%; Preston views it as a big shakeout within a roughly 10-year gold bull market only two years old, citing silver's ~60% GFC drop before a 5x move.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Holders with right-sized positions should not sell into capitulation.
insights.quote: my guess is it's probably a 10-year bull market in gold that we're only two years into

insights.claim: Adam Taggart keeps dollar-cost averaging into precious metals, citing near-universal expert support for owning gold and the persistent loss of fiat purchasing power, and expects a 2027 drawdown rescue playbook to boost metals.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Metals as hedge against liquidity-driven rescue response.

insights.claim: Treasury yields of about 5.05% on the 10-year and 5.40% on the 30-year mean 'there is an alternative'; New Harbor expects potential capital gains as rates fall and sees the S&P priced for poor or negative 10-15 year returns, while Felix Zulauf sees the 10-year falling from 5% to 3%.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Duration offers income and crash protection.

insights.claim: John Lod notes Fed Governor Waller signaled a possible 50bp hike, pushing the DXY to about 103 with potential upside to 108-110, hurting precious metals, while the long bond rallied as markets cheer the Fed fighting inflation.
insights.speaker: John Lod (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Hawkish Fed boosts dollar, pressures metals, supports long bonds.

insights.claim: New Harbor monitors cash's relative strength ranking versus other asset classes; cash has ticked up as stocks, commodities and bonds faltered, a signal seen before major selloffs like 2008-09 and 2002.
insights.speaker: John Lod (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Rising relative strength of cash could trigger further defensiveness.
